skillRating.reasoning: As a Tier 2 midrange Yellow deck, Hisoka-led lists present several real choices each turn: which Gon or Killua to play into the energy line, when to spend AP on Raid upgrades, and what to hold back for the opposing board. Its four-of core and many interchangeable low-cost bodies keep most turns fairly obvious, so the cards carry a lot of the win rate, while Raid AP sequencing and the thin disruption suite mean misplays on the 1- and 2-AP turns can cost the game.

strengths: Naraku appears as three distinct card numbers at 4 copies each, so a Raid payoff is easy to find once a base is on board.
Onigumo gives a dedicated Raid base, letting the deck turn an early body into a bigger threat.
Shikon Jewel Shard at 4 copies helps smooth resources and gives life-area value.
Kagura and Kanna fill the early energy line with cheap characters that carry useful effects, and the Raid sequencing rewards good play.
Goshinki and Kanna's Mirror add some board defense and interaction against attackers.
weaknesses: The Raid plan needs both a base and a payoff in hand, so awkward draws leave the deck stalled in the first turns.
The AP ramp of 1/2/3 slows Raid turns, so the deck gets run over by fast aggro-tempo decks such as Sakamoto Days - Yellow Heisuke Mashimo.
The trigger package is thin, with few defensive options to stabilize when life cards start to fall.
The deck lacks the burst damage of Double Attack or Damage (2), so it often cannot race decks that close the game quickly.
The 14-name list has little room for tech or flexibility, and the Inuyasha card pool is shallow compared with the top IPs.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Compared with other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, Purple Naraku asks for regular decisions each turn: when to deploy the Raid base versus hold it, how to pace the 1/2/3 AP ramp, and when to commit the Naraku payoff. Its Raid sequencing and Naraku's Raid condition mean a misordered turn or a stalled draw costs real tempo, and it is punished by faster aggro-tempo decks, but its key cards are straightforward once a base is on board, so the obvious line wins a fair share of games.

strengths: The large Sesshomaru bodies win BP battles once deployed, and Bakusaiga adds extra pressure to them.
Playing four copies of Kagura, Naraku, Hakudoshi and Kanna gives the deck steady support bodies that build the energy line.
Mid-curve Raid and When Played value from Naraku and Kagura rewards careful sequencing.
The deck is sturdy in grindy midrange matchups where the board stalls and each trade matters.
weaknesses: Slow early development makes the deck vulnerable to aggro-tempo decks like Bomb Devil, Rem and Heisuke, which take life before the big Sesshomaru versions arrive.
Six split Sesshomaru versions dilute copies of the best card, so hands often hold a mismatched high-cost Sesshomaru and too little energy.
Draw and search support is thin, so a bad opening hand rarely recovers.
The deck has almost no removal or Snipe, so it cannot deal with evasive or Impact finishers.
Its trigger package gives little defense, so it loses races at low life.
It lacks the high-end finishing power of top midrange decks like Ichigo Kurosaki and Sung Jinwoo.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Within Standard Union Arena, this midrange Purple deck makes several meaningful choices each turn about when to play large Sesshomaru versions, which energy line to build, and how to sequence Raid and When Played value from Naraku and Kagura, so it sits mid-high on decision density and timing. Its six split Sesshomaru versions and thin draw support make misplays and bad hands costly, while its strong bodies and Bakusaiga let it win on power once the board is set, keeping the autopilot factor moderate.

strengths: Playsets of Inuyasha (042, 043, 045, 046) and three Kagome versions give high odds of curving out from a mono-red energy line with no color problems.
Tetsusaiga at 4 copies gives Inuyasha a persistent BP and pressure boost to win front line battles against mid-sized characters.
Kikyo (049) and I'll Protect You with My Life offer defensive tools that help slow Midrange mirrors.
Sit! and Bone Eater's Well add a little interaction and board development flexibility that suits a grindy, even matchup.
The deck is simple to pilot, with a clear role for each character on the energy line and the front line.
weaknesses: It is slow against aggro-tempo decks such as Sakamoto Days - Yellow Heisuke Mashimo and Demon Slayer - Red Zenitsu Agatsuma, which are ahead on board before Inuyasha's stronger versions arrive.
Only 2 Shippo and 2 Bone Eater's Well makes the cheap early energy-line bodies thin, so some openings stall with a hand of expensive Inuyasha and Tetsusaiga.
Little draw or search means a hand with duplicate Kagome and no Inuyasha leaves the deck without its main attacker.
Without Damage (2), Double Attack, or reliable Snipe, the deck struggles to finish a game against the stronger Midrange builds that stabilise the board.
Trigger quality is low: many life cards reveal weak or situational effects, so taking early hits does not give the swing back.
A very small card pool and a lack of recent top-cut results mean the deck has little room to adapt to a fast-moving field.

main.name: I'll Protect You with My Life

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Red Inuyasha is a straightforward midrange shell: a mono-red energy line with playsets of Inuyasha and Kagome means the obvious curve-out wins many games, so decisions per turn and sequencing traps are modest. Its main skill demands come from choosing between front-line and energy-line plays and from reading matchups against faster aggro decks, which keeps matchup variance and error punishment moderate within the Standard field.

strengths: Playsets of Miroku (068/070/071) and Sango (056–059) give plenty of cheap bodies, so the energy line fills early without missing a drop.
Determine How to Live at 4 copies gives some smoothing and helps find key cards.
Wind Tunnel and Hiraikotsu give the deck targeted interaction and pressure so it can disrupt tempo decks on occasion.
Four copies each of the Miroku and Sango lines make the opening hand predictable and the deck's plan easy to execute.
The deck's low-cost curve avoids awkward AP bottlenecks on turns one and two, when AP is restricted.
weaknesses: The deck has no real finisher; there is no Impact, Damage 2 or Double Attack, so it cannot punish opponents who stumble.
Against the faster decks, Heisuke, Rem and Bomb Devil, it loses the tempo race and its life drops before the setup comes online.
Low trigger quality with only three Barrier copies leaves life cards giving little value when flipped.
Many near-duplicate characters in the Miroku and Sango lines make the deck flood on low-impact bodies in the mid game.
Barely any search or card advantage means a bad draw has no recovery, and a single removal-heavy opponent can grind it out.
The deck is single-color Red with a thin pool, so it has no way to adjust for matchups and cannot keep up with the stronger decks in the field.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Red Miroku is a straightforward midrange deck whose four-copy playsets of Miroku and Sango make the opening predictable, so the obvious line wins a good share of games, which keeps the autopilot score high. Its decisions are mostly about when to commit characters and when to fire Wind Tunnel or Hiraikotsu against the faster Heisuke, Rem and Bomb Devil decks, so decision density and matchup variance sit modestly above the simplest Standard decks. Errors are punished moderately, since losing the early tempo race to fast decks can be hard to recover from but there is little complex sequencing to get wrong.

strengths: Sukuna (SR), (015) and (047) give a deep set of high-BP Raid targets, so the deck can dominate the front line once set up.
Four Yuji Itadori variants (006, 037, 038, 101) provide plenty of cheap bodies to build the energy line and serve as Raid bases.
Domain Expansion (067) and Malevolent Shrine give late-game reach that can close games through blockers.
Playing four copies of every core card keeps draws predictable and the Raid chain repeatable.
Nobara Kugisaki (043) and Takuma Ino fill out the early curve, so energy line development is rarely blocked.
weaknesses: The deck is slow to assemble, so it falls behind fast Aggro-Tempo decks such as Sakamoto Days Heisuke and Re:ZERO Rem before Sukuna lands.
It has almost no draw or search, so hands missing early Yuji or Takuma Ino lose the Raid turn.
Sukuna's Finger and Divergent Fist are the main interaction, and they are too narrow to answer varied boards.
Trigger density is low and offers little defensive value, so early life loss from aggro decks snowballs.
Sitting under 1% of the field means the list is poorly tuned against the current meta, with little proven tech.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Blue Sukuna Raid midrange involves a fair number of Main Phase decisions around energy-line development, Raid setup, and when to commit high-BP targets, but the core plan is fairly linear. Timing matters mainly in sequencing the Raid chain and holding interaction, while misplays in early development are costly against fast Aggro-Tempo decks, which makes errors significant but not razor-thin. Four copies of each core card and strong high-BP bodies mean the deck wins a good share of games on its cards alone.

strengths: Playing 4 copies each of Ultimate Mechamaru and Ultimate Mechamaru, Mode: Absolute makes the Raid payoff reliably available.
Twelve or more Aoi Todo copies across the different versions mean there is always a base or Raid target, and their draw and filtering effects smooth out the draws.
Boogie Woogie and Domain Expansion (100) create swing turns that can fix a bad position, making them a useful backup against stalled boards.
Goodwill Event and Utahime Iori support the hand, letting the deck keep up in longer midrange games.
Positioning decisions around the front line and energy line give a real skill edge to experienced pilots.
weaknesses: The Raid setup is slow on turns 1-3 and loses tempo against Chainsaw Man Bomb Devil, Re:ZERO Blue Rem and Sakamoto Days Heisuke.
Raid needs both a suitable base character and enough energy, so a draw without cheap early characters stalls the plan.
Life-card triggers give little defensive value, so racing decks punish any stumble.
With so many copies of different Aoi Todo versions, some draws are redundant bodies that do little against faster boards.
Opposing removal on the Raided character costs a full turn of AP and leaves the deck with little recovery.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Union Arena Standard decks are generally straightforward to pilot, so this Raid midrange deck sits in the middle of the field: it asks for regular decisions about base selection, energy-line positioning, and when to commit to the Raid payoff, with real but not extreme turn-by-turn branching. Its slow turns 1-3 and reliance on a suitable base plus energy make errors costly against faster Standard decks, while the strong Aoi Todo and Mechamaru density means a reasonable draw still wins without precise play, keeping the autopilot factor moderate.

strengths: Black Flash gives burst damage.
Gojo is a high-BP top end.
Four-of Nobara Kugisaki lines provide cheap energy-line bodies, so energy requirements are met by turn two or three.
Raid chains from Yuji Itadori into stronger versions reactivate attackers and trigger When Played effects, which sustains pressure.
Black Flash gives burst damage that can swing a close damage race.
Satoru Gojo adds a high-BP top end that can win battles against mid-sized attackers.
weaknesses: Outpaced by faster and better-supported lists.
No recent top cuts.
The current meta has faster and better-supported aggro-tempo decks, such as the Sakamoto Days and Evangelion decks, which out-tempo its Raid setups.
Little draw or search leaves it vulnerable to hands with no early energy-line characters or no Raid target.
Triggers rarely stabilize, so falling behind in the damage race is hard to recover from.
Spreading across multiple near-identical Yuji and Nobara versions risks awkward energy and AP requirements in a given hand.

skillRating.label: Advanced
skillRating.reasoning: Red Yuji is a mid-tier aggro-tempo deck whose Raid chains and energy-line sequencing require deliberate turn planning, pushing decision density and sequencing demands above a straightforward beatdown list. Errors are punished because the deck has little draw or search and triggers rarely stabilize, so a misordered Raid or a hand without an energy-line body can lose the race. Its cards do a fair share of the work, but a new pilot would still lose much of its win rate without correct timing and matchup awareness.

strengths: A low curve of Yoji Uruha and Chihiro Rokuhira lets it fill the energy line fast and attack from turn two, which makes the most of the 1/2/3 AP ramp.
Full playsets of several Iori Samura versions make early drops very reliable and minimize dead draws.
Raid chains on Iori Samura give it a lasting board advantage when they work, with the character reactivating and moving up for another attack.
Iai White Purity Style adds a way to push damage through a stalled front line.
I Want to Protect My School Life improves hand quality and consistently smooths the early game.
weaknesses: It struggles to keep up with faster, stronger tempo decks such as Sakamoto Days - Yellow Heisuke Mashimo, whose boards outclass its BP.
It lacks a high-power finisher and rarely gets Impact or Damage (2), so life races drag out.
There is little card advantage, so after a bad trade it runs out of resources against midrange decks like Attack on Titan - Green Reiner Braun.
Trigger value is low, so it cannot rely on a life trigger to swing a close race.
It has almost no removal, so large front line characters from decks such as Solo Leveling - Purple Sung Jinwoo go unanswered.

main.name: I Want to Protect My School Life

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Kagurabachi Purple Iori Samura is a low-curve aggro-tempo deck built on full playsets of Iori Samura, so most turns have one obvious play and the deck is comparatively forgiving to pilot. Its main skill demands are attack timing with raid chains, deciding when to commit to the board against faster or stronger boards, and reading the matchup, which is where its moderate matchup spread and 44 skill ceiling come from.

strengths: Four copies each of several Chihiro Rokuhira cards give a deep name pool for Raid chains, so the deck can reliably find a Raid target on the board.
Kunishige Rokuhira and Char Kyonagi supply early bodies that can build the energy line without needing a perfect curve.
Having several playable Hakuri Sazanami and Togo Shiba numbers gives it plenty of mid-cost characters to fill the front line.
Raided characters switch to active and can be moved to the front line, which lets the deck swing back in the same turn it commits to the board.
Mono-red gives it clear energy requirements, so mid-game turns are rarely colour-screwed once the energy line is set up.
weaknesses: The curve is slow against Aggro-Tempo decks like Heisuke Mashimo, Bomb Devil and Blue Rem, which often take the first few life cards before Raids come online.
A hand with several Raid cards but no base Chihiro to Raid onto leaves AP unspent and falls far behind on tempo.
Few draw, search or filtering effects mean awkward hands cannot be smoothed, which hurts the Player One 1 AP turn the most.
With little Impact, Damage (2) or Snipe, the deck depends on winning plain BP battles, and a blocker with equal BP sidelines its attacker only when the BP is equal or higher.
Cut-down trigger support, with a single Event and few Color or Final triggers, gives it weak defense when its life gets pressured.
Splitting copies across many alternate-art numbers of the same cards suggests an unfocused list that lacks tech for the current field.

main.name: That Day is What Drives Me. You Just Made the Reason Clearer

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Against the other competitive Standard decks, this mono-red midrange list makes several meaningful choices per turn: when to commit characters to the energy line, which base Chihiro to Raid onto, and whether to attack or hold blockers. Its timing demands are moderate, since most sequencing is in its own Main Phase with a few Raid and switch-to-active windows to track. Matchup variance is notable because it is a slow deck that must change plan against aggro-tempo opponents, while the Chihiro Raid chains give it a strong default that keeps autopilot play viable.

strengths: Four Kaiju No. 8 (054) plus three each of (053) and (055) give a thick Raid payoff line, so once the energy line is stable the deck can threaten big BP bodies that win battles.
Playing 4 copies each of Kafka Hibino (060), (061), (062) and a further 3 of (063) means the early plays and Raid targets are plentiful, so the energy line is rarely short of bodies.
Mina Ashiro (041) and Reno Ichikawa (050) provide cheap supporting characters that fill the energy line and keep the AP ramp used on turns 1-3.
Brace Yourself and Now Leave the Rest to Me, at 4 copies each, give consistent event support, and Found You adds an interaction option when the board matters.
Fortitude 9.8 gives a way to push through blockers in the mid-game, which helps the deck close rather than only trade.
weaknesses: The early turns are slow against aggro-tempo decks such as Sakamoto Days Heisuke, Re:ZERO Blue Rem and Chainsaw Man Bomb Devil, which can take life before the Raid payoffs come online.
The list spreads across many Kafka Hibino numbers, so an unlucky draw can have the wrong Kafka for the Raid you need, or too many Raid cards and too few bodies on the energy line.
Few defensive triggers and little life-recovery mean that when the plan stalls, the deck struggles to stabilise through the life area.
Disruption is minimal, so powerful combo-like or Raid-focused opponents can develop freely; the deck only meets them in BP battles.
The deck has a thin tournament footprint, with a single list in the last 14 days, so how it fares against the current meta is not well proven.

main.name: Now Leave the Rest to Me

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this Green Kaiju No. 8 midrange deck asks for regular decisions about when to build the energy line, which Kafka Hibino numbers to deploy, and when to commit to Raid attacks, placing it above simple aggro shells but not at the top of the tier. Sequencing matters for setting up Raid and AP ramp on turns 1-3, yet most turns are fairly direct, and misplays are usually recoverable rather than immediately fatal. The thick Raid payoff line and plentiful bodies let a straightforward pilot win many games, though the close matchups against tempo decks and the spread of Kafka numbers reward experienced play.

strengths: Twenty-four Soshiro copies give the highest redundancy of the Green decks.
Eightfold Slasher is a repeatable pressure tool.
Six Soshiro Hoshina printings (24 copies) make the plan very redundant, so nearly every opening hand has an early body and the line keeps developing.
Mina Ashiro (041) at 4 copies fills the energy line cheaply, so the heavier Soshiro cards can meet their energy condition on time.
Eightfold Slasher (4 copies) gives a repeatable removal and pressure tool that lets the deck win board fights and open attacks.
Now Leave the Rest to Me and Found You give the deck Main Phase options, so AP is used on more than just bodies.
weaknesses: Out-tempoed by Re:ZERO Rem and Heisuke Mashimo.
No Damage (2) or Impact reach.
The fast aggro-tempo decks, such as Sakamoto Days Heisuke and Re:ZERO Rem, can out-tempo it before the Soshiro line is fully developed.
It has little disruption, so it cannot stop setup-heavy decks from assembling their key pieces.
The list has few draw or search effects beyond Found You, so flooding on events or drawing multiple low-impact Soshiro copies leaves it without a decisive turn.
Recovery from falling behind is limited because there is no board wipe or strong comeback mechanic.

main.name: Hoshina-Style Sword-Slay Technique Number Six: Eightfold Slasher
Now Leave the Rest to Me

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other Standard Union Arena tournament decks, this Soshiro midrange list makes a moderate number of real choices each turn around energy lines, AP spending and when to commit, but its redundant six-printing Soshiro core and Mina Ashiro energy plan keep most turns fairly obvious. Timing and error punishment are moderate, since the deck has little interaction on the opponent's turn and its tempo deficit against fast decks is mostly structural rather than a sequencing trap; the draw does a lot of the work, so the autopilot score is high.

strengths: A low-cost opening of Reno Ichikawa and Iharu Furuhashi builds the energy line quickly without wasting AP on turns 1-2.
Sixteen copies of Kikoru Shinomiya across four numbers make a strong threat nearly guaranteed to appear on the front line.
Falling Thunder gives reach and board interaction in the Main Phase when the front line stalls.
Soshiro Hoshina and Kafka Hibino add mid-curve BP that lets the deck pressure slower decks without a Raid.
weaknesses: The deck is outpaced by Sakamoto Days Heisuke Mashimo, Boros and Zenitsu, which develop faster and trade damage more efficiently.
Without Impact or Damage 2 finishers, one well-timed block stalls an attack and the deck loses its damage race.
Trigger support is shallow, so a life-card flip rarely recovers tempo or stops lethal.
The Kikoru package is spread over many near-identical card numbers, which makes hands clunky and the list hard to tune.
A single-color plan with little draw or search leaves the deck with few answers to grindy midrange decks such as Bleach Purple Ichigo.

main.name: Squadron-Style Axe Technique Number One - Falling Thunder
This Is Who I Am Right Now

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Kikoru Yellow Aggro is a straightforward curve-out deck: the opening sequence of Reno Ichikawa and Iharu Furuhashi is largely fixed, and most turns present one or two obvious plays, so decision density sits in the middle-low range for a competitive Union Arena deck. Sequencing matters mainly around when to commit the Kikoru threat and when to use Falling Thunder, while matchup variance is moderate because the deck's role shifts against faster versus grindier opponents. Error punishment is moderate since its weak trigger support and lack of finishers mean a misjudged race can lose, but the deck's raw pressure absorbs many small misplays; the strong autopilot factor reflects that the cards do much of the work when drawn well.

strengths: Sixteen Cinderella copies make for a very predictable, redundant start.
Cheap yellow bodies use AP efficiently on the early ramp.
Heavy redundancy across four Cinderella printings (16 copies) means a Cinderella is almost always available to anchor the board and energy line from the early turns.
Cheap yellow characters such as Little Mermaid, Marian and Abe let the deck fill the energy line without wasting early AP, so 2-AP turns on the 1/2/3 ramp are used efficiently.
The Grave line (009/010/011) adds mid-curve front-line bodies, so the deck can trade evenly in BP battles without relying on one fragile threat.
Playing 4 copies of most card numbers makes hands very consistent in what they do, so mulligans are rarely needed.
weaknesses: Has neither a finisher nor disruption, so it loses to Ichigo Purple and Sung Jinwoo.
Rated unfavorable against most tempo decks.
It lacks a high-damage closer with Impact or Damage (2), so it gets out-raced by decks like Sakamoto Days - Yellow Heisuke Mashimo and Demon Slayer - Red Zenitsu Agatsuma.
Disruption is almost nonexistent, so it cannot stop setup-heavy lists like Solo Leveling - Purple Sung Jinwoo or the Bleach lists from developing.
Few draw or search effects mean flood or poor-curve draws cannot be fixed, and the one optional extra draw per turn costs valuable AP.
With no strong comeback mechanism, a life deficit from an unblocked early assault is hard to recover from; trigger value is just average.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Yellow Cinderella is a redundant, low-variance midrange deck: sixteen Cinderella copies and cheap yellow bodies make most turns obvious, so decisions are mainly about spending AP efficiently and when to commit to attacks. Sequencing is modest, and its lack of disruption and finisher means matchup knowledge matters somewhat, but the deck wins largely from a consistent draw played the straightforward way.

strengths: Four-copy Marian and Rapi lines give reliable cheap characters, so the energy line develops cleanly on the 1/2/3 AP ramp.
Modernia (019) is a strong target to build toward and can win BP battles against mid-sized characters once the front line is set.
Yellow triggers across the 7 life cards give some chance of a swing turn when the opponent attacks.
A stable, redundant core makes the opening hand easy to evaluate and mulligan decisions simple.
Encounter (029) and Memory add event options that smooth turns where the board is already developed.
weaknesses: Fast Aggro-Tempo decks like Sakamoto Days - Yellow Heisuke Mashimo and Re:ZERO - Blue Rem outpace its curve and close the game before Modernia (019) takes over.
The deck lacks a strong finisher or stackable Impact/Damage (2) plan, so games drag and give opponents time to draw out of trouble.
Little search or recursion means a draw without Modernia (019) or Codename: Red Hood leaves a hand of low-impact Marian and Rapi bodies.
Almost no disruption: it cannot answer Snipe, Raid chains or big threats like Solo Leveling - Purple Sung Jinwoo.
Many similar low-BP characters get outclassed in BP trades by the stronger decks currently placing.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Yellow Modernia is a midrange deck whose core lines are fairly stable, so most turns have a clear default play and the redundant Marian/Rapi curve lets a pilot coast on obvious sequencing. Its main difficulty comes from judging when to commit Modernia versus holding resources and handling close BP battles, with matchup-specific pressure from fast Aggro-Tempo decks; within Standard's competitive field it sits in the middle band, with a fairly forgiving autopilot-driven baseline.

strengths: A smooth early curve: Genos (046/047), Silverfang (049) and Suiryu at 4 copies each give many cheap bodies, so the energy line fills quickly.
The 4x King (039/040/041) and King Engine package gives consistent access to its core plan and repeatable setup.
Saitama (061/062) is a high-BP threat that can win battles through opposing blockers and force the opponent to chump or take 1 damage.
Terrible Tornado (111) and Mumen Rider (060) round out a mid-curve that handles opposing Midrange boards.
The 4x It's About Me Taking You On Right Here, Right Now gives a high-impact effect that can swing close combat turns.
weaknesses: It is slow on turns 1-2 on the 1/2 AP ramp, so fast Aggro-Tempo decks like Sakamoto Days - Yellow Heisuke Mashimo get ahead on board before Saitama appears.
Trigger value is low, so it cannot reliably stabilise when damage lands early.
It has few card draw or search effects, making bad draws (too many Kings and no Saitama) hard to fix.
It has almost no disruption, so it cannot stop engine-based decks such as Rurouni Kenshin - Red Kenshin Himura.
Only 2 copies of Mumen Rider and Tank-top Master mean little support for adapting to different matchups.

main.name: It's About Me Taking You On Right Here, Right Now

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Green Saitama is a midrange deck with a smooth curve of cheap bodies, so most turns offer a clear line and only a few real decisions per game, notably when to commit Saitama and how to spend AP. Sequencing matters less than in control-style decks, and the deck's power and simple curve let a newer pilot keep much of its win rate, though close games and slow 1-2 AP starts still reward careful resource management.

strengths: Six Sonic printings at 4 copies each give a very smooth 1-2 energy opening, so the energy line fills on turns one and two without needing a mulligan.
Garou (073) and Boros (080-082) give top-end BP that wins battles against mid-sized characters. Boros Raids can turn an early Sonic into a large attacker.
Wind Blade Leg and Tempest Wind give burst plays that force chump blocks or clear blockers during the Main Phase.
Moving characters and attacking cost no AP, so cheap Sonic bodies can pressure life from the first Attack Phase after they come off the energy line.
Monster Cells at 4 copies supports the deck's mid-game and helps it keep a board as the game grinds on.
weaknesses: Boros is expensive in both energy and AP, so draws with several copies and too few cheap characters stall until the energy line builds.
Few identified Color or Final triggers makes the life area vulnerable to the fastest Aggro-Tempo decks like Sakamoto Days Heisuke and Re:ZERO Blue Rem.
The deck is highly linear and lacks visible draw or search, so a missed Sonic opening or Boros brick is hard to recover from.
Placing Sonic characters on the energy line to fund Boros removes them from attacks and blocks, creating a real tempo cost.
Removal or sidelining effects aimed at the Raid target slow the Boros plan, and the deck has little disruption to answer larger boards.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Red Boros Raid-Sonic is a mid-complexity tempo deck: the pilot must choose between deploying Sonic bodies, funding Boros by sending Sonics to the energy line, and when to commit Wind Blade Leg or Tempest Wind for battle, which adds real per-turn decisions beyond a straightforward curve. Errors are punished because the deck is linear with little draw or search, so a misjudged energy-versus-attack tradeoff or a Boros brick is hard to recover from, though the smooth Sonic opening keeps the simplest lines reasonably effective.

strengths: A low curve of Ferris (042), Ferris (044) and Subaru Natsuki (038) builds the energy line early, so the Crusch Karsten Raid lines come online by the 3 AP turn.
Crusch & Ferris and Wilhelm Van Astrea give strong BP bodies that win front-line battles against midrange decks.
The 4-copy event suite (One Blow, A Hundred Felled; Troops! Follow Those Two Fools!) gives repeatable board interaction and tempo swings.
Ricardo Welkin and the Raid package give flexible follow-ups once the first Crusch lands, so mid-game plays are rarely dead.
Very high copy counts make the opening hands predictable and the deck easy to pilot.
weaknesses: Split across four Crusch Karsten numbers, so a hand can hold Raid cards but lack the specific base character to Raid onto.
Slower than Blue Rem, Heisuke Mashimo and Bomb Devil, which can race before Raid turns come online.
Few draw or search effects, so awkward hands cannot be fixed and the mulligan is the only recovery.
Low representation with no recent top cuts means the deck has had little refinement against today's field.
Life-card triggers are thin, so a big attack sequence cannot be stopped by defensive triggers.
Mono-blue limits tech options, and the deck lacks reach through Damage (2) or Impact to finish when ahead.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other Standard Union Arena tournament decks, this midrange-tempo Crusch Karsten shell asks for a handful of real decisions per turn: sequencing the AP and energy line, choosing when to Raid onto a Crusch Karsten, and timing the event suite for tempo. Its high copy counts and simple early curve make the opening lines fairly obvious, so the pilot's skill matters most in mid-game sequencing and in mulligan decisions. Errors are moderately punished because the deck is slower than the faster Blue decks and has little recovery, but its strong BP bodies and repeatable interaction keep most mistakes recoverable.

strengths: Subaru into Rem Raid gives a fast clock that is about as quick as any deck except Heisuke Mashimo.
Beats slower Blue and Green midrange decks.
Seven Rem variants and seven Subaru Natsuki cards give the deck a reliable Raid pairing, so it can start applying pressure by its second or third turn.
Cheap Subaru characters fill the energy line quickly, which gets the deck's higher-energy Rems usable as soon as the AP ramp allows.
